input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-632: Mobile Robot Programming. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-computer-vision]
Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.

[opencv-documentation]
Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

[rit-csci-632]
This course covers standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization and path planning. Other topics may include multiple robot systems, robot vision and non-traditional and dynamic robots. Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area. Course offered every other year. Prerequisites: CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

beats.claim: CSCI-632 focuses on standard and novel techniques for mobile robot programming, including software architectures, reactive motion control, map building, localization, and path pl
beats.example: Students will implement various algorithms in simulation as well as on a real robot, and investigate and report on current research in the area.
beats.title: Lesson Introduction and Course Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide with the course title, duration (8-12 minutes), and a simple diagram showing the four main modules: Software Architecture, Reactive Motion Control, Map Building/Localization, and Path Planning.

beats.claim: Mobile robot programming relies on modular software architectures that separate perception, planning, and control systems to ensure maintainability and scalability.
beats.example: A typical architecture uses a central controller that routes data between independent modules, allowing each component to be updated without disrupting the entire system.
beats.title: Software Architecture Fundamentals
beats.visualDirection: Show a block diagram with four labeled blocks: Sensor Input, Perception, Planning, and Actuation, connected by data flow arrows.

beats.claim: Reactive motion control processes real-time sensor data to generate immediate navigation commands without requiring a complete global map.
beats.example: When an obstacle is detected, the robot adjusts its heading and speed instantly using a rule-based response function rather than recalculating a full path.
beats.title: Reactive Motion Control Basics
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a simple feedback loop showing sensor input -> decision logic -> motor command, with a note highlighting 'reactive' vs 'planning' control.

beats.claim: Map building algorithms construct environmental representations by fusing sensor observations with existing spatial data to create navigable models.
beats.example: Laser scanners record distance measurements that are triangulated to populate a grid-based map, which is then updated as the robot moves.
beats.title: Map Building Techniques
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison of a blank grid and a populated grid with distance markers, showing how sensor data fills in spatial information.

beats.claim: Localization determines the robot's current position within a map by matching observed features to stored environmental data.
beats.example: The robot compares its camera feed to a pre-mapped image bank and calculates the best match to pinpoint its coordinates.
beats.title: Localization Methods
beats.visualDirection: Show a small inset of a map with a moving robot icon, highlighting the 'current position' and 'matched features' with connecting lines.

beats.claim: Path planning generates optimal sequences of actions that guide the robot from a start point to a goal while avoiding obstacles.
beats.example: A search algorithm explores possible routes, pruning dead ends and selecting the shortest path based on distance and energy constraints.
beats.title: Path Planning Algorithms
beats.visualDirection: Render a top-down map with a start point, goal, and multiple route options, highlighting the selected path in a distinct color.

beats.claim: Students implement algorithms in both simulation environments and on physical robots to validate performance under controlled and real-world conditions.
beats.example: A navigation routine is first tested in a virtual environment to debug code, then deployed on a wheeled robot to measure real-time response times.
beats.title: Simulation vs. Real Robot Testing
beats.visualDirection: Split screen showing a simulation interface on the left and a photo of a real robot on the right, with a checkmark indicating successful deployment.

beats.claim: Students investigate current research in mobile robot programming to identify emerging techniques and contribute to the field through structured reports.
beats.example: A student analyzes a recent paper on dynamic path planning, summarizes key findings, and proposes a modification for classroom implementation.
beats.title: Research Investigation and Reporting
beats.visualDirection: Display a template for a research report with sections for 'Summary', 'Key Findings', and 'Proposed Modifications', using placeholder text.

beats.claim: The course requires prior knowledge from CSCI-630 or CSCI-331 and is typically offered every other year during the spring semester.
beats.example: Students must have completed foundational programming courses before enrolling, ensuring they possess the necessary technical background.
beats.title: Prerequisites and Course Logistics
beats.visualDirection: List the prerequisites and schedule details in a clean, bulleted format on a slide, with icons for a book and a calendar.

beats.claim: Students will evaluate their implementations against a checklist that verifies software architecture, motion control responsiveness, map accuracy, and path planning efficiency.
beats.example: The checklist includes items like 'Modular code structure verified', 'Reactive response time < 100ms', 'Map update frequency consistent', and 'Path deviation within tolerance'.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a simple checklist graphic with four boxes, each containing a key metric and a pass/fail indicator, ready for student annotation.

learningObjectives: Define the core software architecture components required for mobile robot programming, including reactive control loops and modular design patterns.
Explain how reactive motion control algorithms process sensor data to generate real-time navigation commands.
Demonstrate the integration of map building and localization techniques to enable autonomous path planning in dynamic environments.
